title: Rights Group Urges FIFA to Block Infantino Re-Election Bid, Citing Term Limit Violation
excerpt: FairSquare has filed a formal complaint arguing FIFA President Gianni Infantino has already served the maximum three terms, as mounting opposition threatens his decade-long grip on world football.
body:
• Human rights organization FairSquare has urged FIFA's Governance Committee to rule Infantino ineligible for re-election, arguing he has already served three terms — the maximum allowed under FIFA statutes.
  • Infantino claimed in 2022 that his first term (2016-2019) should not count because he completed an interrupted mandate after Sepp Blatter's resignation — a position FairSquare says has no legal basis.
  • The complaint comes amid unprecedented pressure on Infantino after his failed $20 billion World Cup privatization proposal prompted UEFA, CONCACAF, and the AFC to call for a leadership review.
  • The presidential vote is scheduled for March 18, 2027, in Morocco, with several national associations already withdrawing their support.

Human rights organization FairSquare has urged FIFA to rule that President Gianni Infantino is ineligible to seek another term, filing a formal complaint that argues the Swiss-Italian administrator has already served the maximum three terms permitted under the governing body's own statutes.

In a letter sent to FIFA's Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee (GACC), reported by The Athletic, FairSquare said Infantino's claim that his first spell in charge should not count toward the term limit is "inconsistent with FIFA statutes" and sets "a very dangerous precedent."

"The rules state clearly that three presidential terms is the maximum allowed. FIFA can't simply circumvent this rule — which serves as a check on presidential power — by saying that his first term doesn't count."

— Nicholas McGeehan, FairSquare Director

The Term Limit Question

FIFA presidents are limited to three terms in office under rules introduced as part of sweeping governance reforms in 2016. Infantino was first elected at an Extraordinary Congress that year following the resignation of Sepp Blatter amid a corruption scandal. He was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and again in 2023.

In 2022, Infantino successfully argued before the FIFA Council that his initial stint — from 2016 to 2019 — should not count as a full term because he was completing an interrupted mandate rather than serving a term he had been elected to start. The Council unanimously confirmed that interpretation in December 2022, two days before the World Cup final in Qatar.

FairSquare questioned the transparency of that ruling, noting its reasoning was never made public. The complaint was drafted with assistance from Miguel Maduro, the former head of FIFA's independent Governance and Review Committee.

"The principle of term limits was a fundamental aspect of the 2016 reform aimed at limiting power. Trying to carve out an exception reveals how some at FIFA conceive of rules not as rules but as obstacles to be circumvented."

— Miguel Maduro, Former FIFA Governance Committee Head

A President Under Siege

The FairSquare complaint lands at a moment when Infantino is facing the most serious challenge to his authority since taking office. Last week, UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation, and CONCACAF jointly called for a review of his conduct after FIFA proposed creating a $20 billion subsidiary — FIFA Forward Enterprises — linked to its competitions to attract private investment.

The proposal triggered swift backlash. All 55 UEFA member nations threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments if the stake sale proceeded. Carlos Cordeiro, the former Goldman Sachs banker and U.S. Soccer president who had served as one of Infantino's closest advisers for five years, resigned in protest, calling the plan "a bad deal for football."

Sources familiar with the situation told Reuters that the three confederations viewed their joint letter as an opportunity for Infantino to step down with his dignity intact. Several national associations, including England, Wales, Scotland, Serbia, and Sweden, have formally withdrawn their backing for his re-election.

Who Still Supports Infantino?

Despite the mounting opposition, Infantino retains significant support. The African confederation (CAF) and the South American confederation (CONMEBOL) have backed his leadership, and both organizations criticized what they described as a "concerted effort" to undermine the FIFA president.

Infantino's survival may ultimately depend on the many small and developing nations that rely heavily on FIFA's financial largesse. While the sport's traditional powers hold outsized influence, all 211 member nations have an equal vote. Infantino has cultivated relationships across Africa, Asia, and the Pacific during his decade in charge.

Opponents could force an Extraordinary Congress if 20% of FIFA's membership — approximately 42 associations — request one in writing. Such a congress would need to be held within three months, potentially providing a path to remove Infantino before the scheduled election.

Possible Successors

As Infantino's position weakens, several potential successors have emerged, according to Reuters. CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani, a Canadian businessman, is reportedly considering a challenge. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, who boycotted the World Cup final over disagreements with Infantino, and AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa of Bahrain are also seen as potential candidates.

The presidential vote is scheduled for March 18, 2027, in Morocco. What once appeared to be a formality for Infantino now looks increasingly uncertain.
